main.title: Destiny
main.subtitle: Guardians explore a shared science-fiction world through cooperative and competitive missions
main.summary: Destiny is an online first-person shooter video game developed by Bungie.

cards.heading: Bungie launches a shared-world shooter
cards.text: Destiny is Bungie's online first-person shooter, first released on 9 September 2014 for PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Xbox 360 and Xbox One. Players become Guardians, using a power called Light to defend Earth's last safe city and investigate threats on other planets. Bungie combined shooting with role-playing elements in a shared science-fiction setting, where story missions, cooperative activities and competitive matches offer different ways to spend time in the same world.

cards.heading: Guardians, the Traveler and later expansions
cards.text: A Guardian can patrol a destination freely and take part in public events, or enter a three-player strike with a group. Raids increase the group size to six. Competitive modes include both objective-based matches and deathmatch, giving the same underlying shooting another set of goals. The game's activities therefore accommodate different kinds of session: exploring a location, completing a mission together or facing other players in a structured contest.

cards.heading: Reception, publishing and the series that followed
cards.text: Four expansions developed the original release over its first two years. The Dark Below arrived in December 2014, House of Wolves in May 2015, The Taken King in September 2015 and Rise of Iron in September 2016. They added story content, missions and competitive modes, while The Taken King brought broader changes to the game. Originally published by Activision, Destiny moved to Bungie's own publishing after the companies separated in 2019. Its reception combined praise for the shooting with criticism of the story and repetitive progression.

main.title: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U
main.subtitle: Nintendo’s crossover fighter reaches Nintendo 3DS and Wii U in two distinct versions
main.summary: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Super Smash Bros. for Wii U, collectively known unofficially as Super Smash Bros. 4, are two 2014 crossover fighting games developed by Bandai Namco Studios and Sora Ltd. and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 3DS and Wii U video game consoles.

cards.heading: Separate releases on Nintendo 3DS and Wii U
cards.text: Nintendo's crossover fighting series reached Nintendo 3DS and Wii U in two versions developed by Bandai Namco Studios and Sora Ltd. in 2014. Both brought together fighters, items, music and stages from Nintendo and several other publishers. The portable edition arrived first, launching in Japan on 13 September; the Wii U release followed in North America on 21 November. Each version adapted the same central contest: weakening opponents with attacks and knocking them out of the arena.

cards.heading: Crossover fighters and a new balance of combat
cards.text: As part of the Super Smash Bros. series, Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Super Smash Bros. for Wii U are non-traditional fighting games where players use different attacks to weaken their opponents and knock them out of an arena. The games are crossover titles that feature characters, items, music, and stages from various Nintendo franchises, as well as from several third-party franchises. The games began development in 2012 and were announced at E3 2013. The gameplay was tuned to be between that of the faster, more competition-oriented Super Smash Bros. Melee and the slower, more casual-friendly Super Smash Bros. Brawl.

cards.heading: Eight-player battles, amiibo and reception
cards.text: The Wii U version expanded a match to as many as eight players. Both releases introduced playable Mii fighters and supported Nintendo's amiibo figures, while customisable special moves let players alter a character's attack options. Additional fighters and stages followed as downloadable content. Together these features gave the crossover several ways to grow: more people could join a local battle, players could bring their own Miis into the cast, and later releases added further opponents and settings.

main.title: Murasaki Baby
main.subtitle: Take a frightened child by the hand
main.summary: Murasaki Baby is Ovosonico's PlayStation Vita puzzle-platform game, first released in North America on 16 September 2014. The player guides a small girl through a world of children's fears and fantasies by touching her hand and drawing her forward. She carries a heart-shaped balloon, while the unsettling figures and scenery give the journey a deliberately uneasy appearance. The control makes care part of the action. Instead of steering an independent hero with a stick, the player offers a visible point of contact to somebody who may hesitate before following it into the next strange place.

cards.heading: Take a frightened child by the hand
cards.text: Murasaki Baby is Ovosonico's PlayStation Vita puzzle-platform game, first released in North America on 16 September 2014. The player guides a small girl through a world of children's fears and fantasies by touching her hand and drawing her forward. She carries a heart-shaped balloon, while the unsettling figures and scenery give the journey a deliberately uneasy appearance. The control makes care part of the action. Instead of steering an independent hero with a stick, the player offers a visible point of contact to somebody who may hesitate before following it into the next strange place.

cards.heading: Change the background to change what can happen
cards.text: Touching other characters' balloons unlocks backdrops with different powers. Swiping the rear touchpad changes the active background, allowing the player to alter the conditions around Baby while continuing to guide her. Puzzles can require quick movement between those powers, connecting the front and back surfaces of the Vita in the same task. The player therefore handles both the child's immediate progress and the environment that makes it possible. A change in scenery is not merely decorative, because it can transform the practical meaning of an obstacle standing in front of her.

cards.heading: A small Italian studio uses the Vita's particular surfaces
cards.text: Massimo Guarini directed and designed the game after working on Shadows of the Damned. Ovosonico's visual approach draws on illustrated Gothic traditions, giving the child's upside-down face and surrounding creatures a coherent unsettling style. Gianni Ricciardi and Akira Yamaoka contributed music. European and Japanese releases followed shortly after North America. Murasaki Baby gives the Vita's touch controls a narrative purpose: holding a hand and changing the world around it feel like related acts of guidance, allowing the hardware to support the player's relationship with the character rather than simply provide alternative buttons.

main.title: Bayonetta 2
main.subtitle: Return to Bayonetta’s world in the original Wii U adventure
main.summary: Bayonetta 2 is a 2014 action-adventure game developed by PlatinumGames and published by Nintendo for the Wii U.

cards.heading: A new Bayonetta adventure made for Wii U
cards.text: Bayonetta 2 is a 2014 action-adventure game developed by PlatinumGames and published by Nintendo for the Wii U. It is the sequel to the 2009 game Bayonetta, and was directed by Yusuke Hashimoto and produced by Atsushi Inaba, Akiko Kuroda, and Hitoshi Yamagami, under supervision by series creator Hideki Kamiya.

cards.heading: Dodging into Witch Time
cards.text: Bayonetta combines close combat with gunfire against angelic and demonic enemies. Dodging at the last moment activates Witch Time, slowing nearby opponents and creating an opening to retaliate. Weapons can be equipped in combinations on her hands and feet, changing the attacks available during a sequence. Combat grades reward the player for linking combinations quickly while avoiding damage; Pure Platinum is the highest result. Timing a dodge and maintaining a clean sequence therefore matter alongside defeating the enemy.

cards.heading: An opening for Umbran Climax
cards.text: A full magic gauge gives the player access to Umbran Climax. For a short time, Bayonetta's combinations gain extra Wicked Weaves and Infernal Demon summons, extending their reach and damage while restoring health. Activating it turns a stored resource into a burst of power. The timing is left to the player: the same gauge can become a way to press an advantage or recover during a difficult encounter.

cards.heading: Critical acclaim and later releases
cards.text: Bayonetta 2 received widespread critical acclaim, with praise for its combat system, visuals, and overall improvements from the first game. A Nintendo Switch version was released in February 2018. A sequel, Bayonetta 3, was released on October 28, 2022.

main.title: The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel II
main.subtitle: Continue the story of Trails of Cold Steel
main.summary: The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel II is a 2014 role-playing video game developed by Nihon Falcom.

cards.heading: Reuniting Class VII in a country at war
cards.text: Trails of Cold Steel II is Nihon Falcom's 2014 role-playing game for PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita, continuing the first Cold Steel. Rean Schwarzer awakens during Erebonia's civil war to find his classmates scattered across the country. His effort to reunite Class VII takes the party across the world through turn-based battles and encounters shaped by the conflict. A completed save from the previous game can carry choices and relationships into some events and dialogue.

cards.heading: Original PlayStation releases and later adaptations
cards.text: It was first released in Japan for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Vita before being localized into English by Xseed Games in 2016. A Windows port by Xseed was released in February 2018, while a remastered version for the PlayStation 4 was released in Japan in April 2018 and worldwide in June 2019. A port for Nintendo Switch was released in Asia in 2021. A sequel, Trails of Cold Steel III, was released in late 2017.

main.title: Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor
main.subtitle: Follow Talion and Celebrimbor through a world shaped by rivalries
main.summary: Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is a 2014 action-adventure game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Warner Bros.

cards.heading: Talion, Celebrimbor and enemies who remember
cards.text: Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is a 2014 action-adventure game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment. An original story based on the legendarium created by J. R. R. Tolkien, the game takes place between the events of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings film trilogies. The player controls Talion, a Gondorian Ranger who bonds with the wraith of the Elf Lord Celebrimbor, as the two set out to avenge the deaths of their loved ones. Players can engage in melee combat, and use wraith abilities to fight and manipulate enemies. The game introduces the Nemesis System, which allows the artificial intelligence of non-playable characters to remember their prior interactions with Talion and react accordingly in subsequent encounters.

cards.heading: Building Tolkien’s world and the Nemesis System
cards.text: The game's development began in 2011. In order to create an accurate environment and be consistent with Tolkien's books, the developers consulted Tolkien scholars from Warner Bros, as well as Peter Jackson, director of the film trilogies The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit. They also received assistance from Wētā Workshop, who advised on the special effects. Christian Cantamessa served as the game's lead writer, while Dan Abnett was recruited to write dialogues for the Orcs featured in the game. Combat in the game was largely influenced by the Batman: Arkham series, while Monolith had previously experimented with the nemesis system in a cancelled Batman game based on Christopher Nolan films. Gameplay of sports games and pen-and-paper role-playing games influenced the design of the nemesis system, which was intended to create personal stories for each player and generate memorable Uruk-hai characters through gameplay.

cards.heading: The original launch, reception and later releases
cards.text: Shadow of Mordor first appeared on PlayStation 4, Windows and Xbox One in September 2014, followed by Behaviour Interactive's PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 versions that November. Reviewers praised its combat, exploration and Nemesis System, while the story and boss battles drew criticism. Remembered encounters with individual enemies became a central part of the game's reception. Downloadable content followed the launch, and Monolith continued the series with Shadow of War in October 2017.

main.title: Forza Horizon 2
main.subtitle: Return to the Horizon festival across two Xbox consoles
main.summary: Forza Horizon 2 is a 2014 racing video game developed for Microsoft's Xbox One and Xbox 360 consoles.

cards.heading: An open-road sequel developed for two Xbox consoles
cards.text: Forza Horizon 2 is the 2014 open-world racing sequel set around the Horizon Festival in southern France and northern Italy. Players travel between events and explore roads, countryside and hidden barn finds. Playground Games developed the Xbox One version, with Sumo Digital creating the Xbox 360 edition and Turn 10 supporting both. The festival combines organised races with the freedom to drive through its southern European setting, with events taking place by day and at night.

cards.heading: Delisting and the later closure of online services
cards.text: The game was delisted from sale on 1 October 2018, following the expiration of its car branding licenses. The game's online servers, along with those for Forza Horizon, were shut down on 22 August 2023.

main.title: Driveclub
main.subtitle: A road race with a shared result
main.summary: Driveclub is Evolution Studios' PlayStation 4 racing game, first released in North America on 7 October 2014. Its road events combine a direct driving model with the idea of a club whose members contribute to a common reputation. Races, time trials and drifting challenges take place along routes in several countries. The cars remain the central attraction, but the presentation also pays attention to the landscape, light and weather surrounding them. Driving a clean section can matter alongside the position reached at the finish line.

cards.heading: A road race with a shared result
cards.text: Driveclub is Evolution Studios' PlayStation 4 racing game, first released in North America on 7 October 2014. Its road events combine a direct driving model with the idea of a club whose members contribute to a common reputation. Races, time trials and drifting challenges take place along routes in several countries. The cars remain the central attraction, but the presentation also pays attention to the landscape, light and weather surrounding them. Driving a clean section can matter alongside the position reached at the finish line.

cards.heading: Another target inside the same race
cards.text: Optional challenges appear within an event, asking the driver to beat a particular section or performance measure while the larger race continues. These smaller comparisons give a corner or stretch of road a purpose beyond merely reaching the next one. Club progression adds those efforts to a shared total, connecting individual driving with the group's standing. Away from online features, the Tour provides a structured sequence of events. The player learns each car through braking, steering and acceleration rather than managing a detailed simulation of its mechanical systems.

cards.heading: A difficult start and a changing sky
cards.text: Driveclub launched with serious online problems that damaged a game built around connection and shared progress. Later updates expanded it, including dynamic weather that changed both the appearance and conditions of a route. Critics consistently noted the detailed cars, sound and environments, even when judging its early limitations more harshly. Hybrid supplied the score. Sony closed the servers in March 2020 and removed the game from sale. Its offline events remain separate from the club features that originally gave its title and progression their meaning.

main.title: Alien: Isolation
main.subtitle: Observe, listen and survive aboard Sevastopol
main.summary: Creative Assembly's survival horror follows Amanda Ripley through Sevastopol, using sight, sound and cautious movement to evade the Alien.

cards.heading: Learning to Be Afraid of a Corridor
cards.text: Alien: Isolation is Creative Assembly's 2014 survival horror game, following Amanda Ripley aboard Sevastopol. Its technology and industrial spaces draw on Ridley Scott's 1979 Alien. A single creature makes noise, light and movement dangerous: the player watches its behaviour, listens for its approach and chooses when to move or hide. Survival depends on interpreting the station and its sounds while the threat moves through it.

cards.heading: A Future Built With the Past
cards.text: Sevastopol's physical buttons, terminals and bulky tools make its technology part of the action. Using a device requires Amanda to approach it and spend time waiting for a response. While she works, the surrounding space remains a source of danger. A door or terminal can occupy her attention at a moment when the player also needs to watch and listen for movement nearby.

cards.heading: The Monster Has to Feel Present
cards.text: Animators Simon Ridge and Tobias Kleanthous worked to give the creature movement that could shift between slow and fast while retaining continuity. Its posture, distance and speed help the player judge an encounter. The animation has to suggest a body acting within the station, giving visible signs to read while preserving the unease of watching something unfamiliar.

cards.heading: Listening Means Choosing Where to Look
cards.text: Footsteps and movement in the vents can redirect attention before the creature appears. Listening may change a planned route or prompt the player to wait. Sound extends the encounter beyond what Amanda can see, giving the spaces around a corridor or room an immediate importance. A quiet interval leaves the player assessing the next signal and deciding whether to move.

cards.heading: One Alien Replaces an Army
cards.text: Creative director Alistair Hope described a design centred on the vulnerability of the original film. One creature could hold the player's attention through its movements and its possible presence nearby. Doors, desks and vents gain importance because they affect where Amanda can go and what she can observe. Surviving an encounter can mean finding a moment to leave the area safely.

cards.heading: The Motion Tracker Narrows Attention
cards.text: The motion tracker supplies approximate distance and direction, but consulting its screen takes attention away from the corridor ahead. The audible signal creates urgency while the player chooses how long to keep looking at the device. Its information is useful alongside direct observation, with both competing for attention during a crossing or a search for shelter.

cards.heading: Useful Tools Also Produce Risk
cards.text: Running, using a flashlight and activating noisy equipment can draw the creature's attention. Each action has an immediate use and a consequence to weigh: speed helps cross a space, light makes a dark route readable, and a distraction can pull the threat elsewhere. Hope described a reactive creature without a predetermined path. The player learns to judge these signals and adjust plans as the situation changes.

main.title: Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate
main.subtitle: Capcom · Nintendo 3DS
main.summary: Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate is Capcom's expanded Nintendo 3DS hunting adventure, released in Japan as Monster Hunter 4G. A travelling caravan takes the hunter between settlements and dangerous regions, where assignments involve tracking and defeating large creatures. Their materials become weapons and armour for later expeditions. The journey gives each encounter a purpose beyond its immediate reward: a particular creature may hold the part needed to finish a set of equipment. Choosing the next hunt therefore begins with considering what the hunter wants to make.

cards.heading: A caravan follows the next hunt
cards.text: Monster Hunter 4 Ultimate is Capcom's expanded Nintendo 3DS hunting adventure, released in Japan as Monster Hunter 4G. A travelling caravan takes the hunter between settlements and dangerous regions, where assignments involve tracking and defeating large creatures. Their materials become weapons and armour for later expeditions. The journey gives each encounter a purpose beyond its immediate reward: a particular creature may hold the part needed to finish a set of equipment. Choosing the next hunt therefore begins with considering what the hunter wants to make.

cards.heading: The ground is no longer flat
cards.text: Ledges and climbable surfaces give attacks a new vertical dimension. Leaping from higher ground can begin an attempt to mount a monster, turning its movement into another opportunity for the group. The Insect Glaive adds mobility and a companion that gathers extracts, while the Charge Blade changes between weapon forms. Every weapon has its own commitments and recovery times. Learning when a creature is about to turn, charge or pause gives the hunter time to choose an attack that can finish before the next danger arrives.

cards.heading: Prepare for a stronger opponent
cards.text: Four hunters can cooperate locally or online, sharing the work of containing a creature and surviving its attacks. Equipment, restorative items and an understanding of the terrain all contribute to that preparation. Ultimate adds G-rank challenges and more content to Monster Hunter 4, extending the ladder of increasingly demanding hunts. The Western edition arrived in 2015. Progress remains expressed through knowledge and equipment: a familiar monster becomes more manageable when the player recognises its behaviour and brings tools suited to the task.
